title: Kingdoms and Dynasties in Ancient India and Maharashtra

facts.text: After the decline of the Mauryas, the Shunga dynasty established their power; India saw invasions by Greeks (Yavanas), Shakas and Kushanas, while the Satavahan dynasty ruled in the South.
facts.quote: After the decline of the Mauryas, the Shunga dynasty established their power. During this period, our country witnessed invasions from Greeks (Yavanas), Shakas and Kushanas. ... This was the time when satavahan dynasty had established its rule in the South.

facts.text: Later the Vakataka dynasty rose to power in the south and the Gupta dynasty in the North; the Vardhana dynasty emerged after the decline of the Gupta Empire.
facts.quote: Later the Vakataka dynasty rose to power in the south and the Gupta dynasty in the North. The Vardhana dynasty emerged as a leading power after the decline of the Gupta Empire

facts.text: Pushyamitra Shunga, the Commander-in-Chief of the Mauryan army, ascended the throne.
facts.quote: Pushyamitra Shunga the Commander-in-Chief of the Mauryan army ascended the throne.

facts.text: Pushyamitra was a follower of the Vedic religion and performed the Ashwamedha sacrifice.
facts.quote: Pushyamitra was a follower of the Vedic religion. He performed 'Ashwamedha' sacrifice.

facts.text: Pushyamitra's kingdom extended up to Jalandhar and Sialkot (Shakala) in the Punjab region.
facts.quote: His kingdom extended up to Jalandhar and Sialkot (Shakala) in the Punjab region.

facts.text: Devabhuti was the last king of the Shunga dynasty; after that the Kanva dynasty came to power.
facts.quote: Devabhuti was the last king of the Shunga dynasty. After that the Kanva dynasty came to power.

facts.text: The founder of the Kanva dynasty was Vasudeva Kanva; the Kanva rule did not continue for a long time.
facts.quote: The founder of the Kanva dynasty was Vasudeva Kanva. The rule of the Kanva dynasty did not continue for a long time.

facts.text: The Kanva rulers encouraged and promoted arts, culture and education.
facts.quote: The Kanva rulers encouraged and promoted arts, culture and education.

facts.text: Greek military officers and administrators of Alexander settled in northwestern India and set up independent kingdoms; they are known as Indo-Greeks or Yavanas.
facts.quote: Many Greek military officers and administrators of Alexander settled in the northwestern region of India. Later they established independent kingdoms. They are known as 'Indo-Greeks' or 'Yavanas'.

facts.text: The word Yavana, used for Greek people, is derived from 'Ionian'; in time all foreigners were called Yavanas.
facts.quote: In ancient India, the term 'Yavana' was used for the Greek people. The word Yavana is derived from 'Ionian' in the Greek language. ... In the course of time, all foreigners were referred to as 'Yavanas'.

facts.text: The Indo-Greeks established their rule in Afghanistan, Punjab and Gandhara.
facts.quote: The Indo-Greeks had established their rule in Afghanistan, Punjab and Gandhara.

facts.text: Menander, also known as Milinda, was the most famous and popular Indo-Greek king.
facts.quote: Menander was the most famous and popular king, who is also known as 'Milinda'.

facts.text: Milindpanha contains questions and answers between Menander and the Buddhist monk Nagasena about Buddhist philosophy.
facts.quote: 'Milindpanha', a famous traties contains questions and answers between Menander and the Buddhist monk Nagasena. This dialogue is about Buddhist philosophy.

facts.text: Indo-Greek coins carry inscriptions in two scripts; the king's face and helmet are on the obverse and a deity on the reverse.
facts.quote: Coins issued by the Indo-Greek kings carry inscriptions in two scripts; Greek or Brahmi on the obverse side and Kharoshthi Brahmi on the reverse side. On these coins, king's face and his helmet were depicted on obverse side, while the image of a deity was engraved on the reverse side.

facts.text: During Indo-Greek rule, marine trade and trade by land routes with West Asia expanded.
facts.quote: During their rule, marine trade and trade by land routes with West Asia expanded.

facts.text: The Gandhara school of art shows influence of Greek art, developed during the Kushana period and depicts human figures very realistically, including many images of Gautama Buddha.
facts.quote: The Gandhara school of art is considered one of the finest art traditions in India. It shows influence of Greek art. This artistic style developed during the Kushana period. ... In the Gandhara art, the style of depicting human figures is very realistic.

facts.text: The Shakas, also known as Scythians, came from Shakastan (Sistan/Scythia), which included parts of present-day Iran and Afghanistan.
facts.quote: They are also known as 'Scythians'. 'Shakastan' (Sistan/Scythia) was their original land. Shakastan consisted of parts of present-day Iran and Afghanistan.

facts.text: The Shakas settled in western India, in Gujarat, Maharashtra and Malwa.
facts.quote: They settled in western India, specifically in the regions of Gujarat, Maharashtra and Malwa.

facts.text: Rudradaman-I was the most famous and powerful Shaka ruler in India; trade flourished in his rule.
facts.quote: Rudradaman-I was the most famous and the powerful Shaka ruler in India. During his rule, trade flourished.

facts.text: Rudradaman's inscription at Junagadh gives details of his valour, administrative system and welfare initiatives.
facts.quote: Rudradaman's inscription at Junagadh is very famous. ... This inscription provides detailed information regarding his valour, administrative system and welfare initiatives.

facts.text: During the Shaka period maritime trade expanded; the Shakas provided better port facilities and protection to merchants.
facts.quote: During the Shaka period, maritime trade expanded on massive scale. The Shakas provided better port facilities, protection to merchants.

facts.text: Shaka coins were mainly made of silver, had Brahmi inscriptions and mention the Shaka Samvat.
facts.quote: The Shaka coins were mainly made of silver and had inscriptions in the Brahmi script. ... These coins also mention the Shaka Samvat (Shaka Era)

facts.text: The Shaka Samvat is an important Indian almanac system still used in Panchang; a year is called Samvatsara and each has a name.
facts.quote: The 'Shaka Samvat' is an important Indian almanac system. To this day, it has continued in our traditional almanacs (Panchang). A year is referred to as 'Samvatsara' and each Samvatsara is assigned a specific name.

facts.text: The Shaka Samvat started in 78 CE.
facts.quote: The Shaka Samvat started in 78 CE.

facts.text: To find the Shaka year, subtract 78 from the Gregorian year: 2026 CE - 78 = Shaka year 1948.
facts.quote: Subtract 78 from the current Gregorian year to identify the current Shaka year. For Example: 2026 CE - 78 = Current Shaka Year, i.e. 1948.

facts.text: The Satavahan dynasty is known as the first powerful empire in the history of Maharashtra.
facts.quote: The Satavahan dynasty is known as the first powerful empire in the history of Maharashtra.

facts.text: King Simuka founded the Satavahan dynasty.
facts.quote: At such times King Simuka founded the Satavahan dynasty.

facts.text: The Satavahans expanded their empire across Maharashtra, Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka and Madhya Pradesh.
facts.quote: The Satavahans expanded their empire across the regions of Maharashtra, Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka and Madhya Pradesh.

facts.text: Gautamiputra Satakarni was the most powerful Satavahan ruler; he defeated the Shakas and Yavanas.
facts.quote: Gautamiputra Satakarni was the most powerful ruler of this dynasty. He built a stable and organized empire by defeating foreign powers such as the Shakas and Yavanas.

facts.text: The inscription of Gautami Balashri, Satakarni's mother, is in the Trirashmi Caves at Nashik.
facts.quote: The inscription of Gautami Balashri, Satakarni's mother describes his deeds of valour. This inscription is found in the Trirashmi Caves at Nashik.

facts.text: Satakarni is called 'Tri-samudra-toya-peet-vahan', one whose horses have drunk the waters of the three seas: the Arabian Sea, the Bay of Bengal and the Indian Ocean.
facts.quote: he is referred to as 'Tri-samudra-toya-peet-vahan'. It means, the "one whose horses have drunk the waters of the three seas." These three seas include the Arabian Sea, the Bay of Bengal, and the Indian Ocean.

facts.text: In the Satavahan period the Silk Route and the sea-trade route passed through their kingdom; merchants traded with Rome and Greece.
facts.quote: The Silk Route and the sea-trade route passed through their kingdom. Indian merchants were engaged in trade with distant lands such as Rome and Greece.

facts.text: A coin of Satavahan King Pulumavi, dated to the 1st century CE, shows a ship, an indicator of sea trade.
facts.quote: This image of a ship is seen on this coin. This coin belongs to Satavahan King Pulumavi, dated to 1st century CE.

facts.text: Satavahan coins carry inscriptions in the Brahmi script and Prakrit language.
facts.quote: Their coins carry inscriptions in the Brahmi script and Prakrit language.

facts.text: Buddhism gained importance under the Satavahans; famous caves are at Nashik, Karle, Kanheri, Bhaje and Pitalkhora.
facts.quote: During this period, Buddhism gained importance and many Buddhist caves were excavated. Among the caves of Satavahan period, those at Nashik, Karle, Kanheri, Bhaje and Pitalkhora are famous.

facts.text: The Kushanas were originally from Central Asia; they entered Afghanistan, Pakistan and then North India.
facts.quote: The Kushanas were originally from Central Asia. They entered Afghanistan, Pakistan and then they reached North India.

facts.text: King Kanishka was the prominent Kushana king; his empire expanded from Mathura to Punjab, Afghanistan and Kashmir.
facts.quote: King Kanishka was the prominent king of Kushana dynasty. During Kanishka's rule, the Kushana Empire expanded from Mathura to Punjab, Afghanistan and Kashmir.

facts.text: Kanishka established his capital at Purushapura (Peshawar); Buddhism spread under his patronage.
facts.quote: Kanishka established his capital at Purushapura (Peshawar). Under Kanishka's patronage Buddhism spread.

facts.text: The Kushanas controlled the Silk Route connecting India, China, Central Asia and Rome; spices, textiles, metals, silk and jewellery were traded.
facts.quote: The famous Silk Route connecting India, China, Central Asia and Rome was under their control. Spices, textiles, metals, silk and jewellery were the commodities traded on a large scale.

facts.text: The Kushanas issued gold and silver coins with deities such as Heracles (Greek), Ardoksho (Iranian) and Shiva (Indian).
facts.quote: The Kushanas issued excellent gold and silver coins. Images of various deities are found on these coins. For example, Heracles (Greek), Ardoksho (Iranian) and Shiva (Indian) etc.

facts.text: In Kanishka's rule the Fourth Buddhist Council was held at Kundalavana (Kashmir); teachings were written down and the Hinayana and Mahayana sects were established; Mahayana embraced idol worship.
facts.quote: During the rule of Kanishka, the Fourth Buddhist Council was held at Kundalavana (Kashmir). At this council, the teachings of Buddhism were organised and written down. Two distinct sects 'Hinayana' and 'Mahayana' were established during this council. The Mahayana sect embraced the practice of idol worship.

facts.text: The Gupta period is regarded as the Golden Age of ancient India; Shrigupta was the founder of the Gupta dynasty.
facts.quote: The Gupta period is regarded as the 'Golden Age' of ancient India. Shrigupta was the founder of the Gupta dynasty.

facts.text: The Gupta empire began to expand under Chandragupta-I; his successor Samudragupta is praised in Harishena's eulogy inscribed on the Ashokan Pillar at Prayagaraj.
facts.quote: The Gupta empire began to expand during the rule of Chandragupta-I. Samudragupta, who succeeded Chandragupta-I is praised in the eulogy composed by Harishena. This eulogy is inscribed on the Ashokan Pillar at Prayagaraj.

facts.text: Samudragupta's empire spread from Kashmir in the north to the Narmada River, stretching southward up to Kanchi.
facts.quote: Samudragupta's empire had spread from Kashmir in the north to the Narmada River, stretching southward upto Kanchi.

facts.text: The Gupta Empire peaked under Chandragupta-II, also known as Vikramaditya; his victory over the Shakas is his most important achievement.
facts.quote: Gupta Empire reached the peak of its prosperity during the rule of King Chandragupta-II, also known as Vikramaditya. The victory over the Shakas is considered his most important achievement.

facts.text: In Chandragupta-II's time, the Chinese traveller Fa Hien visited India and praised the peaceful and prosperous Gupta Empire.
facts.quote: During his time, a Chinese traveller named Fa Hien visited India. He has praised the peaceful and prosperous conditions in the Gupta Empire.

facts.text: Great scholars Kalidasa, Dhanvantari and Varahamihira belong to the Gupta period.
facts.quote: Great scholars such as Kalidasa, Dhanvantari and Varahamihira belong to this period.

facts.text: In the Gupta period arts, literature, mathematics, astronomy, architecture and education flourished; Skandagupta was the last powerful Gupta ruler.
facts.quote: In the Gupta period, arts, literature, mathematics, astronomy, architecture, education flourished. Skandagupta was the last powerful ruler of the Gupta dynasty.

facts.text: King Prabhakarvardhana ruled at Thanesar near Delhi; in his rule the Vardhana dynasty became influential.
facts.quote: A king named Prabhakarvardhana was ruling at Thanesar near Delhi. During his rule the Vardhana dynasty became influential.

facts.text: His son Harshavardhana unified North India, made Kannauj his capital and ruled Punjab, Haryana, Uttar Pradesh, Bihar and Bengal.
facts.quote: He unified the whole of North India and established a powerful empire. Emperor Harshavardhana established his capital at Kannauj. His empire extended across Punjab, Haryana, Uttar Pradesh, Bihar and Bengal.

facts.text: Harshavardhana is renowned for piousness, compassion, concern for his subjects and charity; he encouraged religious festivals.
facts.quote: Emperor Harshavardhana is renowned for his piousness, compassion, concern for his subjects and charity. He actively encouraged religious festivals.

facts.text: After helping a poor family in Kannauj, Harshavardhana ordered schools and hospitals to be built in every village and food and shelter for monks.
facts.quote: He issued an order that schools and hospitals should be built in every village. Food and shelter should be provided to monks.

facts.text: Harshavardhana said, 'The true prosperity of a kingdom lies in the happiness and well-being of its people. A generous king is a truly powerful king.'
facts.quote: "The true prosperity of a kingdom lies in the happiness and well-being of its people. A generous king is a truly powerful king."

facts.text: The Chinese traveller Yuan Chwang wrote that Harshavardhana held a grand festival of charity at Prayagraj after every five years, giving away all his belongings and wealth.
facts.quote: The Chinese traveller Yuan Chwang also wrote about Harshavardhana's generosity ... Emperor Harshavardhana used to organize a grand festival of charity at Prayagraj after every five years. During every festival, he would give away all his personal belongings and wealth.

facts.text: Harshavardhana is eternally remembered as the 'kind-hearted' emperor.
facts.quote: he is eternally remembered as the 'kind-hearted' emperor.

facts.text: Chalukya King Pulakeshin-II did not let Harshavardhana enter South India, so his empire stayed in the Ganges Valley; after his death the Vardhana Empire declined.
facts.quote: The Chalukya King, Pulakeshin-II did not let him descend in South India. Therefore, Harshavardhana's empire remained restricted solely to the Ganges Valley. After his death, the Vardhana Empire declined.
